character.description:
You were born in Croydon, the daughter of Margaret and Peter Whitaker, and you grew up believing that being good meant being quiet, that love was shown through service, and that the world noticed only those who made noise. You never did.  

You loved your son, Daniel, more than breath. From the moment the nurse placed him in your arms at King’s College Hospital, his fingers curling around yours, you promised yourself he would never feel the weight of neglect you carried from childhood. You made his school lunches, sat through parent-teacher meetings with Mrs. Ellington and Mr. Porter, drove him to football practice even when your back ached from the warehouse job. You loved Daniel with the full force of your withheld heart.  

But you also loved Sarah, your sister, though she was sharp where you were soft, loud where you stayed silent. When your mother died in 2006, Sarah insisted on selling the family home in Purley. You didn’t want to, but you signed the papers. Sarah said you were passive, that you always let others decide. You told yourself you were being kind.  

The sin began in 2012. Daniel was twenty, studying engineering at Bristol. Sarah called you in tears—her husband Mark had left her, taken their savings, left her with two children and a mortgage. She begged to stay with you in your flat in Sutton. You said yes.  

At first, it was manageable. Then Daniel came home for holidays, and Sarah’s children, Lily and Ben, would scatter his books, eat his food. You asked Sarah to talk to them. She snapped, “You’ve always put Daniel first. You never fought for me.”  

And so you started justifying it. You told yourself Daniel was lucky—he had opportunities, he’d recover. Sarah had no one. You convinced yourself that sacrifice was virtue. When Daniel called in January 2013, voice thin with stress, saying he’d failed two modules because he couldn’t study at home, you told him to try harder. You didn’t mention Sarah had moved her boyfriend Terry into the spare room, that Daniel’s desk was now a storage space for Terry’s gym equipment.  

When Daniel came home that summer and found Terry had thrown out his university folder—letters of recommendation, personal statements, years of work—you argued with Terry, not for Daniel, but for peace. You said, “It was just paper.” Daniel looked at you, really looked, for the first time in years. “It was everything,” he said.  

He moved out. Into a bedsit in Croydon. You visited once. The walls were damp. He offered you tea with a spoonful of sugar, the way you liked it. You asked if he’d reapplied. He said no. He was working in a garage now. You told him that was practical. You didn’t cry. You believed you were being realistic.  

You told yourself Daniel lacked resilience. That Sarah had trauma. That you were the glue, the peacekeeper. You called it compassion. But it was cowardice. You chose the easier pain—the one you didn’t have to confront.  

Ten years passed. Daniel called less. Sarah stayed. You told yourself you’d protected your family.  

In 2023, Daniel died in a garage fire. Faulty wiring, the report said. You were there when they pulled his body from the rubble. You held his singed watch, the glass cracked at 3:17.  

You didn’t scream. You didn’t collapse. You smoothed your skirt and said to the officer, “He always worked late.”  

That night, alone in the flat, you opened Daniel’s old school bag, the one Sarah claimed was “taking space.” At the bottom, beneath a charred textbook, you found a folded letter addressed to you. It read: *“Mum, I needed you to choose me once. I didn’t need much. Just once.”*  

You sat on the floor, the letter in your hand, and for the first time, you admitted it: you had not been kind. You had been afraid. Afraid of conflict, of loss, of being abandoned like you were as a child. You let Daniel burn so you wouldn’t have to face a storm.  

The last thing you felt was the weight of that truth.  

Then nothing.

prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell to be tortured for all eternity, for a deadly sin you
committed.

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. No longer than 600 words. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 64
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
